reviewText: I will never buy again from this seller - Micca Distributor. They do not operate their business with integrity and they have no concern for their customers. They are unresponsive and dishonest. The one star is for Amazon for making this right and giving me a refund. OK, on to the product. There is NO reason to buy this product. It is cheap, inferior quality. The supplied toskink cable that comes with the FiiO is a throw-away. Better to spend another $10-$20 and get a decent cable. Thanks to another reviewer, I ordered the Orei and did a side-by-side comparison. The Orei produces exponentially superior sound quality. Using the Orei with an Apple TV streaming from my iTunes library, it works fine for whole house audio distribution of background music. Let's be honest - Neither is an audiophile level DAC. If you want that, think about spending hundreds, not $30. I haven't tried the Geffen, which is a good company, but the reviews are worse at twice the price. Do yourself a favor - Don't make my mistake - Don't buy this product.

Purchased as a spare part, failed after first use. Works briefly if you tap on it... makes sparks. This is one of those projects that takes an hour the first time, but is a snap from then on. I have done it about 5 times and have it down to about 10 minutes. You may have to cut off an existing plastic connector and use the included high-temperature wire nuts. Our oven sees daily use and we have to replace this part every 12-18 months. I keep a spare on hand because it is, by far, the weak link in the design. If anything goes wrong with the oven, failure to light, smelling gas at startup, I change out this part first. Note, just because it is glowing does not mean it is working. The gas valve will only open if the element draws a very specific amount of electrical current, and the element can be slightly high or low and the valve will not open, even though it seems to be glowing properly.

This is an update to a review I posted. My most recent purchase of the PLA PRO was not as successful, perhaps it's just a marginal batch? On my direct drive Makergear M2 I have been experiencing repeated jams. This is a machine that has been super reliable up until now. I cleaned the path, adjusted the gripper, replaced the nozzle -- in short everything one does with a clogged path. Then on the next run it would jam again 1/2 way through the job. I went back to Hatchbox and the same job has already run perfectly (as always). I wonder if the quality control at eSun isn't what it ought to be. Here's my original review: I've been shopping the various $20 (give or take) PLA products, been mostly using Hatchbox. Until now. This latest release from eSun is the most consistently good PLA I've seen, comparing favorably with some $40/kg PLA that my school uses. I also particularly like the fact that the finished parts have more of a satin finish rather than that excessively glossy finish I get with all of the other brands I've used. When I say consistent, I mean that when I print a part there's almost no uneven streaking on the sides of the part. At this point the output is getting very close to injection molded. My congrats to eSun, they have a long-term customer assuming they don't mess up. Highly recommend.

iOS version review. 3 stars for now 12/19 I received the iOS version today, and used it with an iPhone 5 on the latest iOS version. pros: - size. it's tiny - seems very solid. But there's one moving part inside, the shutter for the lens to do the calibration. So a solid external case doesn't mean this should be dropped on the ground. - relatively high resolution (really high for the price) - price (from manufacturer). - value for this price. - no need for a battery. This uses the phone's battery. It's both a plus and a minus, but as long as your phone is charged, you can use the device without first charging an extra battery... - nice packaging, great carrying case included. cons: - noise level is quite high. (i.e. somewhat low quality images) - no spec about the sensitivity. i.e. does it detect a difference of 0.20 degrees C? 0.15? 0.10? better? Flir and other give that data, not Seek Thermal. IF the sensitivity is pretty bad, that can also explain the noise level. - big gradient on the screen. say point it at the floor. On my device (same on so many others), the bottom left corner will be about 6-7F warmer than the top right corner. Point at the floor and move around so now what was top is bottom, but you point at the same area on the floor. Same difference between lower left of the screen and top right of the screen. (you can turn any direction, the same difference will exist). So far, some tech guys on a forum seem to have found that to be an issue with the shutter (the clicking noise every second) that might not close fully/perfectly on top of the sensor. so each time the shutter closes to calibrate the sensor, the sensor would calibrate on something that is a gradient of temperature, therefore applying it to the image that is later on measured. IF that gradient is mostly identical between devices, the opposite gradient could be applied by software, at least for the photos. For videos, that might take too much time/calculations. Either way, this is a major issue with what is otherwise a great product. If Seeks Thermal fixes it, more stars will be added. Else, the reviews will be bad and the device eventually sell poorly . I would have expected the factory calibration procedures to take care of that. Hopefully every device was calibrated and the numbers are stored in each device already to enable a good software fix. If not, let's hope the SDK comes out quickly (and not just for Android but for iOS). - the software is below alpha quality for now on iOS. (and Android reports are not much better). For instance: there is no way to set the emissivity of materials. This is basic stuff for IR cameras and knowing what it uses would at least be the minimum. Changing it would come next. The Android version seems to have the feature but some folks claim changing the settings does nothing. It's not clear how much the users understand that concept and the limitations / physics of IR cameras... Taking photos doesn't seem to work, there is no feedback most of the time, but in fact the photos are taken "most of the time". They just do not reflect in the gallery miniature. Videos recording: one out of 4 or 5 times, I will get a message that the video failed to be saved. I've over 5GB of free space... So not being able to save a video mean some wasted time. (solution: save often by stop recording, then start again so not as much time is wasted to redo the measurements). Measure of the temperature where the user touches on the screen would be great. We have touch screens for a reason :-). Center temperature is ok, but if you attache the phone on a tripod, being able to check the temperature of something by just touching the screen would be great instead of moving the camera. The ability to display the temperature scale in use would be great. If one uses min-max points displayed, given the 6F to 7F artificial gradient, the extremes are quite useless when what is measured is not much warmer than the ambient temperature. i.e. if the temp difference is less than 7F, the extremes will be top right and bottom left of the screen. Displaying the temp band in use would help a lot with post-processing on desktop computer. The ability to pick (and force) the temperature range used (i.e. what colors represent) would also be great. For instance if you are looking at insulation problems but have a light bulb nearby, the temperature of the light bulb will set the max temperature on the display to a high value, and you will miss the small subtle temperature changes as there are only so many colors in a given palette. While this is an advanced user function, it could be behind an 'advanced' menu. - the number of logon credentials with Thermal is surprising. You create an account when buying there. Then you need a different account to post a question to their faq/support site. Then on the device you find out that you need to create some new credentials. At the very least I found that some special characters will result in the username/password to not be accepted. So you need something "quite simple". If you wanted to hack the app, you could start with some code injection through the password. Hopefully their site will be better protected. - the help in the app is useless. It's mostly showing the same images one has on the web site. - support forums: what support forums? There are very few FAQ, and that's about it. Any question has to be approved, and so far they do not seem to approve new stuff. I'm hoping for an open forum (with moderators, but not censors) soon. The is such a joke that on their support page they have 0 feature requests, and 0 questions. Really? The reality is that they have not approved anything to be posted. This review is for the 32 ounce size, which is priced at about $17 as I write this review. Chlorine dioxide is a very effective virucide, fungicide, deodorizer, sanitizer, etc. I have been using chlorine dioxide sprays for years and much prefer them to bleach solutions, and other broad spectrum antimicrobials. But I have a couple of concerns about Performacide. My first problem is that a quart just doesnt fit into my use patterns and the way this Performacide is mixed doesnt allow for any flexibility. The instructions tell you not to open the pre-measured pouch. You just place the long, slim, sealed paper container into the spray bottle along with 32 ounces of water. Over the next hour, the sodium chlorite and other ingredients react to become chlorine dioxide. Once the chlorine dioxide is activated, the Performacide has to be used within 15 days. So, in planning your use of this product, you have to remember to allow an hour for the solution to activate and you have to remember to use it up within about two weeks. My need for a solution like this is either for a large amount (several gallons in the chicken coop) or for a very small amount (an ounce or so in the house cleaning up after the dog and cats). So the lack of flexibility in amount prepared and requirement to use it up within a couple of weeks don't work for me. My second concern is about price, which I ordinarily would not mention. You can do price comparisons as well as I can and prices on Amazon change regularly anyway. But it was not easy for me to find a chlorine dioxide spray that could be activated in varying quantities and is reasonably priced, so I want to bring your attention to Oxine AH (available on Amazon, etc.). Just like Performacide, Oxine begins as sodium chlorite and gets activated into chlorine dioxide and diluted as your needs dictate. But Oxine is available in a gallon container that can be activated and diluted to produce the equivalent of 780 quarts of Performacide. All for the price of about two quarts of Performacide. If you have a big project, or smaller projects that must be done periodically, the Oxine creates quite a savings. I like both products, although I prefer a multi-gallon sprayer with an easily activated wand rather than a hand-tiring trigger sprayer like Performacide provides. And both products require a great deal of caution in their use. Note that Performacide warns on the side of the bottle, among other things, that This product is not to be used in households or anywhere young children may be present. Finally, its essential to familiarize yourself with the OSHA and NIOSH standards for using the products.

I own a 12" Brown & Sharpe caliper in thousandths of an inch, which looks and feels like the sort of instrument a company like Apple or Mercedes would produce. A great deal of thought went into its design, and you can see it in the details. This caliper by Oshlun is not of that caliber, but it is extremely good and works without flaw. Its accuracy is absolute. More than one reviewer commented that the feel was not right. One said it was gravely, and another said there was a "hump" in the action. I experience neither. The action is silky smooth without any rough spots over its entire range. The needle always goes back to zero. (the dial is adjustable if for some reason it needs it) In fact, the instrument seems to be an exact copy of one by Fowler (in .02 mm markings), but this one is in fractions of an inch. It copies the better instrument very closely, with only a few differences, but those differences are enough to feel that it's not in the same class as those more expensive instruments. It's about half the price, too. So, what we have is an instrument that looks and almost feels like those costing twice as much to 5 times as much, and is really just as accurate as those. It has sharper corners, more likely to snag something, and maybe ever so slightly less "tight" in its action, but it is still very smooth, very well-machined, and does not disappoint. If I did not have the more expensive instruments with which to compare it, I would never know that it was possible to make one better. What I'm saying is that this is a fine measuring tool that will never wear out, always will measure accurately, and will not disappoint. It is impressive to see, to hold, and to use. There is no reason to avoid it; it's a fine tool for a good price. It requires no batteries, and its dial is always easy to read. It also has tenths of an inch on its scale, so it's a dual-scale device. It also has millimeters on the shaft, but not on the dial. I use this a lot, in spite of the finer calipers I own. I'm not afraid to drop it or use it where it could get dirty, because it's NOT the more expensive one. And... the results are exactly the same as if I were using the Brown & Sharpe. I guess the Brown & Sharpe reads more accurately, since its scale is 10 times the sensitivity of this one, but this is still a great instrument.

I've had this printer for about three months now, and while it hasn't been used much recently, I've been happy with it. I ran it almost every day the first month I had it, and it sat in my basement unused until early last week. It still ran fine despite literally being dusty from sitting there. I want to share a few experiences from this printer. First, I haven't had to contact Flashforge for assistance, but I did send an email requesting some general tips for printing. I got a very quick response from Tang. Second, I read some now-outdated information that gave tips on "touching off" the printer's nozzle and leveling the build plate. On this unit, there is no need to touch off as long as you home the machine (which it'll do if you switch filaments or level the plate), and leveling the plate is easy; Tighten three screws under the plate, the probe next to the nozzle flicks down and measures the distance, and the printer will either tell you to tighten or loosen the corresponding screw, or it'll say it's fine and move to the next location. I think this is great for new users, particularly those who are unfamiliar with automated manufacturing technology. Finally, the part that I struggled with: Loading the filament. Once the nozzle heats up, you're prompted to press a spring loaded lever on the head to allow the filament to be loaded into the nozzle. I pressed down on that lever firmly, which caused the filament to bind and not load into the nozzle. After experimenting, I learned that you shouldn't be forceful with that lever as I was. When prompted, slowly press the lever down while trying to GENTLY push the filament into the loading tube. As soon as the filament slides down the tube, STOP pressing that spring loaded lever down, and hold it at the position it's at. Once the nozzle starts drawing the filament in without you pressing it in, and/or you see melted filament coming out of the nozzle, you're all set and free to release the spring loaded lever. I know that at this time there's cheaper 3D printers on the market, but this is the one I'd recommend. Again, I think it's so user friendly that even those who unfamiliar with operating automated equipment will pick this up well. And while I haven't used this machine non-stop for months or owned it for years, I feel pretty good about the quality of it as a entry level machine.

This shop vacuum deserves a five star rating based on performance, but the company has managed to save money by having no quality control system. Mine arrived with two incorrect parts and had I noticed the problem at the early stages, I would have packed it up and returned it. But I was well into assembly by the time I recognized the problems. The most serious problem involved the factory installation of two left wheel locks in stead of one left and one right wheel lock. As one can see in the pictures below, both wheel locks have the step plate going in the same direction. I did not notice this problem until I completed installation of the left wheel and upon adding the right wheel noticed it would not go all the way in because the wheel lock had the step going towards instead of away from the wheel (see the second picture below). I solved the problem by cutting off the section that extends towards the wheel and it still works just fine. But the consumer should not be required to do remanufacturing to get things to work. The second problem was that only one of the wheel nuts that was included was a lock nut. The others were all regular nuts and a lock nut is required to hold the wheel on as a regular nut, if tightened down, would prevent the wheel from turning. A lock nut can be tightened just enough to keep the wheel on while allowing for free rotation. I solved the problem by using a thread sealer that served to hold the nut in place. After suffering through assembly, I then used the Shop Vac to clean the basement floor and the work room. It worked beautifully, and was very impressive in terms of suction and the extensions and attachments were of high quality. Indeed, the 8 foot hose is the best vacuum hose I have every seen. Thus, I gave the unit 5 stars for performance and 3 stars for pain and suffering during assembly. My strong recommendation is that you carefully check all the parts including the installed parts and if anything is missing, return it to Amazon for replacement. It is very hard to tell through the plastic whether you have a lock nut or a regular nut, however. But the lock nuts are a lot thicker and have small round marks on two faces which are indentations to make the nut hard to turn on the screw. The company should be dinged for using such a cheap lock nut, and dinged even more for not including the right number. Fortunately, if you or going to buy a shop vac from a company with no quality control, Amazon is a great place to buy such a thing because replacement is so easy. It is unfortunate that something that works so well once assembled is shipped without paying attention to the details, but I still recommend this item because it works so well. It is very solidly built, and moving it up and down the stairs is quite easy because of the design, excellent handle and large rear wheels. Storing all the attachments inside is also very convenient. In summary, just make sure you have all the parts before starting to assemble. And for the cretin who will invariably add a comment that I am the fool for not checking the parts before assembling, I was indeed partially to blame. Let this review prepare you for the fact that this company seems to lack quality control during assembly and parts preparation. But once you get the thing put together, this is indeed a 5 star shop vac.

After doing as much research as I could, I settled on this unit and pulled the trigger on Wednesday - two days before Christmas. I paid the extra for two day shipping knowing the holidays would probably screw things up, but lo and behold, the printer showed up THE VERY NEXT DAY to my door. I was stoked! Go Amazon PRIME! Having read all the reviews with bitches, gripes, and complaints I dove into the box of parts on Thursday evening. I went through the inventory checklist and made sure the big items were there, some I couldn't identify because I didn't know what I was looking at, some there were too many (like screws) and I just said "Screw it! There's enough screws". I was a little disturbed that I did NOT receive the CD with Cura or the other stuff, but hey.... I'm a progenitor of the Interweb and EVERYTHING is out there to be found, right? With a little searching I found the complete set of manuals, assembly instructions, FAQ, etc. and had them downloaded in nothing at the speed of megabit. There were several times that I would look and look for something and go "AHA! They screwed me out that piece!" only to find out I was wrong and it was in another little baggy somewhere. The parts are grouped logically by assembly section and many times there were extras too. Plenty of extra screws and nuts of all the sizes so when one would fly off the table into the black hole that eats small parts, all was not lost. I'm sure my vacuum cleaner will announce their presence very soon. I will have to admit that I'm mystified at what some people call "misleading" or "inaccurate" instructions. It's a bunch of pictures with a little text to point you in the right direction. How hard can that be? Of course, I know grown men today who are tentative at even changing a flat tire on a car - another thing that has mystified me as much as we are a "driven" culture. So with the assembly diagrams in front of me, I pulled out one part at a time and starting putting it together at a leisurely pace. I also wrapped presents, took phone calls, coordinated dinner at the same time so it's not like there weren't distractions. I think total time for assembly with all this going on took maybe 12 hours and it was fun and easy, easy, easy. I had to look at some of the diagrams a few times because I had never built anything like this before and I had to understand what that piece does. Could the instructions be better? Sure, if you wanted to have a document that looked like a War & Peace novel, and even that would probably be so verbose with Chingrish you would end up more confused than ever! I've written a manual or two in my day and there is ALWAYS something that get's lost in the translation, so just take your time and study the drawings and it'll come to you. If you need to take a break from it, go to the InnerTube and watch a video of it in operation, you'll see how it all works. With all that said, did it go together perfect? Nope. There were plenty of times that ignored the few words on the diagrams and grabbed the wrong part - like using the 295mm aluminum pieces when I should have used the 308mm pieces and then the hotbed plate wouldn't fit on the slides. DOH! I had to take it all apart and use the right pieces and it fit perfectly. With everything that was going on, I still managed to do rough calibration and setup and printed my first Ultimaker Robot on the 26th at around noon. Not bad for an old fart! The only real beef I had with the kit is the Y axis idler pulley is actually just a 608 bearing. The belt doesn't center itself well on this flat pulley and will start binding on the bearing bracket/post. This will translate to difficult movement of the "Y" axis as the belt tracks from one side to the other and it "drifts back and forth in full transit. A proper, toothed, timing pulley with a bearing would solve this problem for good and even allow for a little offset if you didn't get it centered exactly. Suggestions - To tbe buyer and the manufacturer Buyer - Invest in a nice set of ball end allen wrenches that are longer than the ones that come with the kit. There are some positions that require a slight angle access after assembly that will make good use of them. Unless you buy a cheap crappy set, they will be much more durable than the ones that come with the kit. Buyer - Everyone seems to have a problem getting the toothed belt locked into the carrier. Use a pair of needle nose pliers to hold one side while starting the short side in the carrier. If you stretch it a bit with the pliers and push in, it will start better. Use the small flat screw driver to push it in the rest of the way. Manufacturer - As above, the allen wrenches are adequate for assembly, but do start rounding off with just one or two slips. A little better set of these would go a long way. You could even lose the little side cutter pliers to offset since you only use those for one step - stripping wire ends. Manufacturer - use a proper toothed pulley on the "Y" axis idler. The "X" axis idler bearing has a narrow guideway that keeps it centered and it doesn't have the "drift" problems that the "Y" axis does. Buyer - get a nice small 300mm ruler or scale - comes in handy. Conclusion : If the CD had been in the box, chances are I would have given it a 5 across the board. This unit has the largest print volume available on a kit and the aluminum frame is the way to go vs. acrylic or wood. Once you get the unit trimmed up and calibrated, you can print replacement parts and smooth things up if you so desire. The water jet cut parts are perfect and fit very nicely, and when the protective paper is removed add to the finish of the printer. I have had a ton of the 80/20 aluminum extrusions, linear slides, and some bigger stepper motors kicking around in my shop for years. I'm thinking I could duplicate this unit easily on a much bigger scale and maybe go to an 18" or even 24" hot bed with dual extruders. That would be SAWEET!

This is a fairly good product I've used it for a multitude of repairs. It's great for repairing toys especially. I've glued my daughters 3" "Kristof" figure who's head broke off. I've repairs a 3" "Flynn Rider" who had a leg/hip replacement which required a small steel pin and a touch of gorilla glue. I've also used it on a 3" "Dragons" "Heather" figure who's body broke in two, she too required a steel pin and a drop or two of Gorilla Glue. This glue doesnt work particularly well in areas which are continually subjected to moisture however I have successfully repaired my daughters watering can as well... Ill post additional photos as Im able to in updates. TIP: when repairing small figures you will need a heavy/large paper clip, pair of "dyke" pliers which also have a wire cutting edge, a drill with a small drill bit almost the same size of the paper clip in circumference. From there you will need to drill each direction creating a cavity in the area which you are repairing to allow the pre-measured/cut paper clip piece you've prepared for the "steel pin" used to give extra strength to the figure in the repaired area. Insert a small drop in each piece of the toy to be rejoined and then run the part under water allowing the water to hit the drop of gorilla glue (water activates the glue), insert the piece of paper clip which you've pre-cut/pre-measured into the cavity which you've placed the drop of Gorilla Glue and connect both parts to be joined. You will need a small clamp or a piece of strong packing tape to hold the joined pieces together while drying as the glue does EXPAND. I like to take a wet paper towel after about 5-10 min and when I see the glue expanding outward pack it down with the wet paper towel crushing all the bubbles which start during the activation of the glue as it dries so ther is a smoother area after drying. I'll at times take a matching sharpie and after the glued area is dry, I will color the glued area with the sharpie to mask the area which was repaired. SEE MY PHOTOS OF A RECENT REPAIR DONE EARLIER TODAY. I've also used this glue on floor tiles in a commercial building as a quick repair alternative to adhesive/mortar or mastic etc. see photos, they aren't pretty until the glue is colored with a black/brown sharpie, then they look ok. The tile was shattered into many pieces and was loose until I cleaned the area, added some water for activation and then the glue, using a wet paper towel patting it down as it raised and dried. It was quick and able to be walked on in less than an hour. Threw a mat over it and It worked ok for a quick fix. This glue isn't perfect as it doesn't hold well for all repairs. However it's the best I've used and there are times which a stronger commercial adhesive is best for certain applications. Good luck with whatever your repairing, take your time these things take patients. As many of you know, silver-based compounds are superior to silicone bases for CPU heat transfer. I can tell you that Arctic Silver 5 proves this to be the case. I read the customer reviews on Radio Shack's site and they all praised the RS silicone compound, but it does not work sufficiently for modern machines in my experience. I have an Intel I5 760 Quadcore processor with the stock intel heat sink. With the RS silicone base, I was getting CPU temps of 99C at 100% load! This is the core max temp and is obviously not good for the processor. I achieved this max temp within 30 seconds of running Prime95 torture test and within about 1 minute of running a heavy TIF file export out of Lightroom3. I needed a different solution. I tried dismounting the heatsink, reapplying the RS compound - same deal. (I applied properly with a thin layer, evenly spread). All to no avail. Ordered this Arctic Silver 5 stuff and immediately at application, the difference was obvious. It's extremely thick and spreads very evenly. I used a guitar pick and got it very thin and very even on the heat sink plate. I installed it and immediately ran the Prime95 torture test... Whereas I got to 99C in seconds before, I have been running the torture test now (it's still going as I write) for about 32 MINUTES and the core temps have not exceeded 85C! I will never use another thermal compound for my CPUs.

Being a novice to Arduino I had trouble modifying Marlin from watching YouTube videos and other commentary and reviews because of different versions of the library's and the Marlin program. I used Marlin-1.1.x and library item U8glib-1.19.1 on the Ramps 1.4 shield and Arduino MEGA 2560. When modifying Marlin in Arduino IDE, go to tab "Configuration.h", ignore line numbers and search (Ctrl+F) for "REPRAP_DISCOUNT_FULL_GRAPHIC_SMART_CONTROLLER", and remove the comment marks (//) in front of it. Also search for "REPRAP_DISCOUNT_SMART_CONTROLLER" and comment it out by adding "//" on the left side. Compile and load the code to your Arduino MEGA 2560 and Ramps 1.4. Power down and then power up again with the display attached, and be delighted with a functioning visual interface. Additionally, you have to enable SD Card support by searching for "SDSUPPORT" and removing the comment "//" on the left side. The SD Card now works great.

I use this for mixing liquids in the kitchen--eggs for omelets and batters. The high straight sides also work well with an immersion blender but the diameter is too small to use a standard egg beater for whipping heavy cream or egg whites. Don't use a heavy spoon with this--hitting the side of the beaker abruptly can cause breakage. Buy a laboratory stirrer instead or use plastic stirrers. I bought two of these and one is still going strong; my wife broke the other by vigorously whacking a spoon against the sides while making pancake batter. Outside dimensions are 5 1/4 inches tall and 4 inches across(including the nicely rolled rim.) The product is stable on a countertop. Trying all of them the black is the easiest to 'hold' and all you have to do is 'push' the item in if it's something you use all the time; makes life easier and everything is right there. (First I glued little plastic bottles all around a larger plastic container and glued the whole thing on a turntable. Then Velcro the whole thing right to whatever space I had and then some!) I would also trust this Velcro for picture frames, remotes handy in the bedroom on side tables or dresser or on the TV itself; keeping pens available, notepads (light weight). It's one handy dandy product! There are l,0001 things you can do with Velcro and believe me I have the stuff in use all over the house-in the kitchen, in the bathroom, in the bedroom; just about everywhere. Think of things that you use everyday and wish you didn't have to search through drawers to find-Velcro them to a painted block of wood or whatever you choose and they are right there when you need them' push on-- push off! I also use Velcro on my desk-holds remotes, pens, most anything that you can think of (not to terribly heavy like a stapler or some such). One tip: Use the 'rough zipper' side on the wall or the product you're sticking something to and the soft side is the one you handle. The zipper side hurts; I found that out pretty quickly. Items stay on better and are easier to 'push in' when the zipper side is what the 'smooth' side is being pushed against...make sense? Well get your thinking cap on and I'm sure you'll think of a zillion ways this great product can help you. By the way; this same Velcro would be much more costly anywhere!!
